extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Kant); educated general readers interested in aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's criteria for aesthetic (taste) and teleological judgements: how to recognise beauty, purposiveness, and the proper grounds of aesthetic evaluation according to the Critique of Judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The judgement of taste is aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: "The judgement of taste is aesthetical." — To decide whether anything is beautiful we refer the representation not to the Understanding for cognition but to the subject (the Imagination, perhaps with the Understanding) and to its feeling of pleasure or pain; therefore the judgement of taste is not a judgement of cognition and is consequently not logical but aesthetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: an aesthetic judgement must be grounded in the subject's feeling (pleasure/pain) rather than in objective concepts. Example contrast: apprehending a purposive building cognitively vs being conscious of satisfaction in that apprehension. Anti-pattern: treating a judgement of taste as a logical, concept-based judgement about the object's properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: The satisfaction which determines the judgement of taste is disinterested
rubrics_metrics.description: "The satisfaction which determines the judgement of taste is disinterested." — When judging beauty we must be indifferent to the existence or utility of the object; the satisfaction invoked is not an interest (not tied to desire, possession, or usefulness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: a pure judgement of taste requires disinterested pleasure — one must not be motivated by personal desire, practical use, or by the object's existence. Examples: preferring or disliking a palace for practical/ethical reasons is irrelevant to a pure judgement of beauty. Scoring note / anti-pattern: any mingling of interest (even slight) makes the judgement partial, not a pure judgement of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: The satisfaction in the PLEASANT is bound up with interest
rubrics_metrics.description: "The satisfaction in the PLEASANT is bound up with interest." — What pleases the senses (the pleasant) is tied to sensation that excites desire and inclination; it is subjective sensation that leads to gratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: if the pleasure arises from sensory gratification that produces inclination or desire, classify it as 'pleasant' not 'beautiful.' Distinguish objective sensation (perception of e.g. green meadows) from subjective feeling (pleasantness) which calls for desire. Anti-pattern: conflating pleasantness (sensory enjoyment) with aesthetic beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: The satisfaction in the GOOD is bound up with interest
rubrics_metrics.description: "The satisfaction in the GOOD is bound up with interest." — That which pleases through a concept (reason) is 'good'; goodness involves concepts of purpose or will and is thus connected to interest (practical concerns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: if approval depends on concepts, purposes, or suitability for volition, treat it as moral/practical 'good' rather than aesthetic. Example: calling something 'good' requires a concept of what the object ought to be; this is not required for calling something beautiful. Anti-pattern: using reason-based or utilitarian grounds as the basis for aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as purposiveness without concept (formal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: An object is called purposive when its representation is immediately combined with the feeling of pleasure; this purposiveness is not a property perceived in the object as such but a 'subjective formal purposiveness' — the conformity of the object's form with the cognitive faculties (Imagination and Understanding) without reference to a determinate concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: beauty is judged when form (not matter/sensation) elicits a free play or harmony between Imagination and Understanding, producing disinterested pleasure. The judgement does not supply a concept of the object; rather it registers purposiveness of form. Scoring note: beauty depends on this 'formative' harmony and not on whether the object serves a purpose for desire or cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure from discovery of unity in nature's empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery that heterogeneous empirical laws or phenomena can be combined under one comprehending principle yields a marked pleasure (often admiration); this reflects a felt harmony of nature with our cognitive faculty and is a ground for aesthetic pleasure in nature's purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: scientific or intellectual pleasures in comprehensibility (finding unity/principles) count as a kind of aesthetic pleasure tied to purposiveness for cognition. Example: being pleased when diverse natural phenomena are subsumed under a single explanatory principle. Applicability: especially relevant to judgements about natural beauty or the aesthetic appreciation of scientific understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement claims universal validity despite being empirical
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the judgement of taste is empirical (a feeling) and thus subjective, it nonetheless claims validity for everyone because its ground — the purposive harmony of the cognitive faculties in reflection — is a universal (though subjective) condition of reflective judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: a proper judgement of taste is accompanied by a claim that 'everyone ought to agree' because the pleasure rests on conditions of reflective judgement shared by all. Caveat: the claim of universality is not derived from a concept but from a presumed common form of cognitive faculties; does not amount to objective necessity in the cognitive sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between aesthetical (formal) and teleological (real) purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic (formal) purposiveness: judging nature's form as purposive by means of feeling (taste). Teleological (real) purposiveness: judging natural products (e.g., organisms) as if they had real purposes, judged by Understanding and Reason according to concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: determine whether a judgement concerns 'formal purposiveness' (beauty, decided by taste/pleasure) or 'real purposiveness' (objects judged as natural purposes, e.g., organised bodies, decided by conceptual/teleological judgement). Application note: natural beauty is assessed aesthetically; functional or organism-like products are assessed teleologically and require conceptual/empirical grounds rather than mere feeling.
